title: Security under load — spoken follow-up
situation: In a technical discussion, someone proposes bypassing authorization in a benchmark. You must answer aloud accurately without overstating the evidence.
instructions: Say aloud why disabling authorization for a benchmark invalidates its result, without making the proposer defensive.

vocabulary.meaning: measuring the system in the configuration it actually runs in, since removing a layer measures a system nobody deploys
a component left out of a measurement, whose own cost then disappears from the reported figure

expectedElements: What the shortcut actually measures is stated
The omitted layer is identified as a real cost
A workable alternative protocol is proposed
modelAnswer: I understand why it is tempting, and I do not think the proposal is careless: authorization adds noise to a measurement. But disabling it measures a system we never deploy. Every request in production passes through that check, and the check itself costs something, sometimes a token validation and a lookup. Removing it moves that cost out of the number we then quote. So the figure would be real evidence for a question nobody asked. What I would run instead is the same benchmark with a pre-issued token, which keeps the layer in place and removes the variability you were trying to avoid. Would that work for your timeline?
commonMistakes: Rejecting the shortcut without acknowledging the noise it was meant to remove
Failing to name the omitted layer as a real cost in the reported figure
variants: Answer again when the deadline leaves time for only one benchmark run.
